items.title: Kenya, Aga Khan University explore partnership to advance Universal Health Coverage
items.description: Kenya, Aga Khan University explore partnership to advance Universal Health Coverage Kenya News Agency
content: Health Cabinet Secretary (CS) Aden Duale has held a strategic engagement with the leadership of Aga Khan University (AKU) at its global headquarters in Karachi, Pakistan, to explore practical areas of collaboration in advancing Kenya’s Universal Health Coverage (UHC) agenda.

The meeting, hosted by AKU Global President and Vice-Chancellor Dr. Sulaiman Shahabuddin, Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) Kenya Diplomatic Representative H.E. Amin Mawji, and senior university faculty, focused on translating the longstanding Kenya–AKDN partnership and existing cooperation agreements into measurable improvements in healthcare delivery for Kenyans.
In his remarks, the CS acknowledged the contribution of the Kenya–AKDN development cooperation framework, which has extended healthcare services to hundreds of thousands of people.

He also noted the significant role played by Aga Khan hospitals in Kenya through their participation in Social Health Authority (SHA) financing arrangements, supporting access to quality healthcare through publicly funded schemes.
The discussions further explored a joint research and innovation framework covering health-system implementation, noncommunicable diseases, maternal and newborn health, and digital health.

Both sides underscored the importance of ensuring that research undertaken in Kenya complies with national legislation, secures local ethical approval, involves Kenyan co-investigators, and delivers meaningful value to the communities concerned.

On strengthening service delivery, the engagement identified opportunities to improve clinical referral systems, enhance patient follow-up in their respective home counties through Community Health Promoters (CHPs), and expand specialist outreach to underserved communities.

“The partnership will also explore supporting public health facilities to strengthen quality assurance and patient-safety practices in line with internationally recognised accreditation standards,” added Duale.

Equally, the two institutions also examined opportunities to strengthen biomedical engineering capacity for the maintenance of public health equipment and advance interoperable digital health systems aligned with the Digital Health Agency (DHA).
“Such integration will support more efficient verification of claims, minimise rejections, and help address processing backlogs within the Social Health Authority (SHA),” the CS assured.

Meanwhile, AKU’s international expertise, research capacity and established healthcare network present an important opportunity to strengthen Kenya’s health system, enhance the national Community Health Promoter (CHP) network and translate successful innovations into scalable interventions and evidence-based national policies.

The CS was accompanied by Kenya’s High Commissioner to Pakistan, Lt Gen (Rtd) Peter Njiru; Dr Ahmed Mohammed, Chief Executive Officer of the Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB), and other senior government officials.

items.title: Kirinyaga County expands healthcare infrastructure
items.description: Kirinyaga County expands healthcare infrastructure Kenya News Agency
content: At least 23000 Kirinyaga County residents are set to benefit from improved access to healthcare following the launch of three projects targeting maternal and child health, outpatient services and primary healthcare delivery.

Governor Anne Waiguru launched the projects, comprising the groundbreaking of a Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (MNCH) Unit at Kiamutugu Hospital and the opening of Kiandieri and Mathia dispensaries, in an initiative aimed at reducing the distance residents travel to access medical services.

The projects are expected to improve access to affordable healthcare while reducing the financial burden on households that have been spending money travelling to distant health facilities for treatment.
Speaking during the launch, Waiguru said the investments aimed at ensuring residents received quality medical services closer to their homes, irrespective of their economic circumstances.

“The projects will bring healthcare services closer to the residents, ensuring that they access quality healthcare when they need it, regardless of their location or economic circumstances,” she said.
She noted that the three facilities would expand access to maternal and child health services, outpatient care, preventive healthcare, laboratory services and essential medicines.
One of the major investments is the construction of the MNCH unit at Kiamutugu Hospital, which is being undertaken through a partnership between the county government and the M-Pesa Foundation.
Upon completion, the new unit will increase the hospital’s bed capacity from seven to 37, providing an additional 30 beds for mothers and newborns requiring medical attention.

The facility will have an operating theatre, newborn unit, antenatal ward, mother and child welfare clinic, laboratory and pharmacy, enabling the hospital to provide comprehensive maternal and newborn healthcare services.

The expanded capacity is expected to strengthen the hospital’s ability to manage deliveries, maternal complications and newborn conditions while improving access to specialised services within the county.
Waiguru said the project was part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn healthcare, building on investments already made at Kerugoya County Referral Hospital and South Ngariama Hospital.
The county has established a specialised MNCH department at Kerugoya County Referral Hospital and operationalised a fully-fledged maternity wing at South Ngariama Hospital.
It has also incorporated modern MNCH units into the ongoing upgrading of Kianyaga and Kimbimbi hospitals, whose construction works are 95 per cent complete.

The Governor said sustained investment in maternal healthcare had contributed to a reduction in maternal and newborn deaths, with maternal mortality declining from 88 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2017 to 49 deaths per 100,000 live births. Neonatal mortality has also dropped from 26 to 11 deaths per 1,000 live births.

She said the county was committed to further reducing preventable maternal and newborn deaths through improved infrastructure, skilled healthcare personnel, specialised care and efficient referral systems.

Waiguru also highlighted the importance of partnerships between government and the private sector in accelerating healthcare development and improving service delivery, citing the near-completion of Mutithi Maternity Wing.
Meanwhile, the opening of Kiandieri and Mathia dispensaries is expected to address the challenge of accessing basic medical services among residents in the surrounding communities.

Some residents previously walked as far as seven kilometres to reach the nearest health facility, a situation that has particularly affected expectant mothers, children and families seeking routine medical attention.

The two dispensaries will offer antenatal and postnatal care, immunisation, family planning and child welfare clinics. Residents will also access cancer screening services, HIV testing and treatment services, tuberculosis screening and care, laboratory investigations and pharmaceutical services.

The availability of these services at the community level is expected to improve access to disease screening, diagnosis and treatment while reducing the need for residents to travel to distant hospitals for medical attention.
Waiguru said expanding primary healthcare facilities was essential in reducing pressure on referral hospitals while strengthening preventive and promotive healthcare at the community level.

The County Government has previously operationalised several dispensaries and laboratories across Kirinyaga, including Kavote, Mucagara, South Ngariama, Matandara, Riakithiga, Kamwana, Kiamwathi, Kianjiru, Umoja, Kiaumbui, Joshua Mbai, Kiandai and Kiandagae.
In addition to expanding primary healthcare, the county is strengthening its referral system through the upgrading of Kimbimbi and Kianyaga hospitals to Level Four facilities, with ongoing equipping.
To ensure the expanded infrastructure is supported by adequate personnel, Waiguru said the county had deployed 116 additional healthcare workers during the current financial year.

Kenyan Researchers Secure Funding to Study Climate’S Impact on Health
items.description: By Jean-Pierre A.
content: Scientists led by the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) have received £2.3 million (about KSh 394 million) to study how heat, drought, malaria, snakebite, hunger and mental distress pile up on the same households in Turkana County. The researchers say these overlapping burdens have gone largely unmeasured.
The three-year study, Strategic Health Integration for Equitable and Localized Decision-making (SHIELD), is funded by the UK-based Wellcome Trust.

“A single family may face heat from outdoor work and a poorly insulated home, food and water shortages, mosquitoes breeding around water points, and snakes in grazing and water-collection areas, all at the same time,” said Dr Daniel Kwaro, the study’s principal investigator.

Dr Kwaro said that, to the best of his knowledge, this is the first project to consider these risks together, because health and weather systems record them separately. Drought is logged without information on who is exposed, and clinics record illness without its link to the climate.
“Heat illness, from fainting to heatstroke, is rarely recorded as heat illness, and even when a clinic sees it, the link to the weather is usually lost,” Dr Kwaro said.
Dr Patrick Amoth, Director General for Health, said the government needs this evidence because the country’s health information systems are built to count diseases one at a time.
“If we, as a government, cannot see that burden, we cannot plan or budget for it, or act before it becomes a crisis,” Dr Amoth said at the launch of the project today in Nairobi.

Over three years, researchers will survey refugee and host households across four seasons, fit 100 adults with smartwatches to measure heat strain, trap mosquitoes monthly, survey snakes in areas where people are bitten, and compare clinic records with what households report. With Turkana County and humanitarian agencies, the team will turn the findings into a climate-health dashboard, a budgeting tool and an early-warning system that can help governments plan.

Dr Gilchrist Lokoel, Turkana County’s Chief Officer of Health, told reporters at the launch that the county was waiting for the evidence, given the sharp changes it has seen in drought, heat and heat-related illness.

Malaria is one of the risks the study will track. Dr Eric Ochomo, head of entomology at KEMRI and a member of the SHIELD team, said a rise of about one degree Celsius had let mosquitoes thrive in places where they were not traditionally found. Anopheles stephensi , a malaria mosquito native to South Asia and the Middle East, was first confirmed in Kenya in 2022 and has since been found in 13 counties, he said. Dr Ochomo said the response would need community awareness as well as science.

“Covering tanks, screening inlets and draining spillage at tap stands and boreholes would stop stored water from breeding mosquitoes, and that work belongs in malaria control, including surveillance for species of mosquitoes, such as the Anopheles stephensi,” Dr Ochomo said.

The researchers describe Turkana as a “sentinel” setting. It does not represent the whole country or continent, but it lets them study how overlapping risks build up, with lessons for similar dryland and refugee-hosting areas.
